The fire has burned roughly 250 acres as of 2 p.m., according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. It has also burned multiple homes.EvacuationsMandatory evacuations were ordered for San Juan Zones 4, 5, and 10 and San Clemente Zones 12 and 13.

“If you are in one of these zones, leave immediately,” the Orange County Fire Authority wrote on X. The evacuation zones include a swath of hillside neighborhoods bordered by the 5 Freeway, Ortega Highway and Avenida La Pata.

It also extends down into neighborhoods closer to the coast and bordered by the 5 Freeway and Camino Los Mares. You can find a map of the evacuation zones on the Orange County Sheriff’s Department website.

articles.headline: City Controller Subpoenas 2028 Olympic Organizers for Financial Records
articles.dek: Los Angeles City Controller Kenneth Mejia issues a subpoena to LA28, demanding detailed financial information and contracts related to the 2028 Summer Olympics.
articles.lead: Los Angeles City Controller Kenneth Mejia has issued a subpoena to the organizers of the 2028 Summer Olympics, LA28, demanding access to the organization's financial records. The legal demand includes requests for bank statements, venue construction plans, and details on contracts with outside vendors.
articles.takeaway: Los Angeles City Controller Kenneth Mejia issues a subpoena to LA28, demanding detailed financial information and contracts related to the 2028 Summer Olympics.
body: Los Angeles City Controller Kenneth Mejia has issued a subpoena to the organizers of the 2028 Summer Olympics, LA28, demanding access to the organization's financial records. The legal demand includes requests for bank statements, venue construction plans, and details on contracts with outside vendors.

This action follows LA28's rejection of a previous request for similar information made by Mejia's office approximately two and a half weeks prior. Mejia stated that the information is contractually obligated to be provided to the city under the 2021 agreement governing the relationship between LA28 and the host city.

LA28 spokesperson Jacie Prieto Lopez indicated that the organization had not yet received the subpoena and therefore could not provide a formal response. She expressed disappointment, suggesting that the city's actions were diverting attention from the essential work of preparing Los Angeles for the Games.

Mejia emphasized his responsibility to protect taxpayer dollars and assess the city's financial exposure from hosting the Olympics. The subpoena aims to ensure transparency regarding spending and revenue as the city could be liable for significant losses if the Games do not break even, with the city covering the first $270 million and any amount over $540 million.

Previous reviews by The Times and city officials have noted that LA28's annual reports have sometimes provided vague or incomplete information, particularly concerning venue progress and contracts exceeding $1 million. LA28 had previously cited potential competitive and partnership risks as reasons for withholding some contract details.

articles.lead: Immigration advocates and Los Angeles officials expressed concern Friday that a reported increase in federal immigration raids is intended to intimidate immigrant communities and suppress their participation in the upcoming midterm elections. Jeannette Zanipatin, policy director for the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights of Los Angeles (CHIRLA), stated that the timing of these actions, so close to the election, is not coincidental and aims to silence voters and divide neighborhoods.

body: Immigration advocates and Los Angeles officials expressed concern Friday that a reported increase in federal immigration raids is intended to intimidate immigrant communities and suppress their participation in the upcoming midterm elections. Jeannette Zanipatin, policy director for the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights of Los Angeles (CHIRLA), stated that the timing of these actions, so close to the election, is not coincidental and aims to silence voters and divide neighborhoods.

Angelica Salas, executive director of CHIRLA, blamed the Trump administration for attempting to discourage voting and announced that the organization and others will deploy legal observers across California as part of the Can’t Stop California campaign. Salas urged voters not to be intimidated, emphasizing the importance of their voices and the state's commitment to protecting immigrants' right to participate in elections.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Chandler Rebel, stated that individuals in the country legally and not breaking laws have no reason to fear. Rebel also issued a warning to noncitizens who vote in U.S. elections, stating they will be apprehended and face consequences, including deportation.

Despite previous assurances from the Department of Homeland Security that agents would not be sent to polling sites, President Trump has previously indicated a willingness to take necessary steps to ensure election integrity. Immigration advocates have raised concerns that increased raid activity could deter people from voting, noting a rise in detentions this summer compared to the previous year.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass accused President Trump of using the raids as a distraction from domestic issues like rising gas prices and his foreign policy. Bass encouraged voters who feel fearful to cast their ballots by mail and stated she is working to increase protections by having the Los Angeles Police Department document federal enforcement activities.

Councilmember Imelda Padilla reported that her district has been significantly impacted by the raids, describing the activity as chaotic and unprofessional. She urged community members to support their neighbors by offering assistance with transportation, groceries, or escorting children to school.

articles.headline: California Voters to Decide on $11.25 Billion Housing Bond Proposition 1
articles.dek: Proposition 1 aims to address the state's housing and homelessness crisis by funding various housing initiatives, including affordable units, veteran loans, and infrastructure.
articles.lead: California voters will consider Proposition 1 in November, a ballot measure proposing an $11.25 billion general obligation bond to fund housing construction and address the state's homelessness and affordability crisis. Supporters argue the state desperately needs this funding to build more homes and alleviate the significant shortage of affordable housing, where over 180,000 Californians are currently homeless.
articles.takeaway: Proposition 1 aims to address the state's housing and homelessness crisis by funding various housing initiatives, including affordable units, veteran loans, and infrastructure.
body: California voters will consider Proposition 1 in November, a ballot measure proposing an $11.25 billion general obligation bond to fund housing construction and address the state's homelessness and affordability crisis. Supporters argue the state desperately needs this funding to build more homes and alleviate the significant shortage of affordable housing, where over 180,000 Californians are currently homeless.

The proposition allocates funds to several key areas: $7.2 billion for acquiring, building, or renovating apartment buildings, with a portion reserved for low-income households and supportive housing for the homeless. This segment alone could help support up to 40,000 rental units. Additionally, $1.25 billion is earmarked for helping veterans secure home loans, and $1.1 billion for low and moderate-income households to purchase homes.

Further funding includes $500 million for infrastructure supporting new housing, such as water and transportation improvements. The bond also designates $450 million for farmworker housing, $350 million for student housing at UC and CSU campuses, and $200 million in grants for tribes to develop housing. Another $200 million will support pilot projects for low-cost housing developed by cities and counties.

Repayment of the bond is estimated to cost the state between $500 million and $600 million annually for approximately 25 years, funded by the state's general fund. The portion for veteran housing is designed to be self-repaid through loan payments from participating veterans. Critics, however, question the reliance on bond financing and argue that only a small fraction of the funds are directly allocated to veterans, despite the bond's name.

Supporters, including housing developers, veterans groups, and legislative leaders, emphasize the urgent need for investment, pointing to stalled projects that lack sufficient funding. Opponents, primarily Republican legislators, express concerns about increasing state debt and suggest alternative methods for housing development.

attribution.originalTitle: There’s a $11.25 billion housing bond on the ballot this November. Here’s what you should know

faqs.answer: Proposition 1 proposes an $11.25 billion general obligation bond.

faqs.question: How will the state repay the funds from Proposition 1?
faqs.answer: The state plans to repay the bond costs, estimated at $500 million to $600 million annually for 25 years, from its general fund, with the exception of veteran housing funds which will be repaid by participating veterans.

articles.headline: California Sues National Archives Over Facility Closure
articles.dek: The state is taking legal action to prevent the closure of a San Francisco facility, citing potential harm to tribal records and lack of consultation.
articles.lead: California has filed a federal lawsuit against the National Archives and Records Administration, seeking to halt the closure of its San Francisco facility. The state argues that the abrupt announcement of the closure, made without consultation with tribes, state officials, or local entities, would irreparably harm California's interests.
articles.takeaway: The state is taking legal action to prevent the closure of a San Francisco facility, citing potential harm to tribal records and lack of consultation.
body: California has filed a federal lawsuit against the National Archives and Records Administration, seeking to halt the closure of its San Francisco facility. The state argues that the abrupt announcement of the closure, made without consultation with tribes, state officials, or local entities, would irreparably harm California's interests.

Tribal governments rely on the National Archives for essential records, including those related to the Bureau of Indian Affairs, such as enrollment, land records, and federal boarding school files. The lawsuit contends that transferring these fragile and historically significant documents risks damage and loss, and will render them inaccessible for an unknown period.

Tribal leaders and historic preservation officers have expressed dismay, stating they were not consulted on the closure plans. While the Archives have since held virtual "listening sessions," participants felt the decisions were already finalized, leading to concerns about transparency and trust.

For many tribes, access to these records is crucial for healing from the trauma of the federal Indian boarding school era and for pursuing federal recognition. The potential inaccessibility of these documents is a significant concern for elders who may not have the time or resources to travel to view them before they are moved.

The lawsuit asks the court to compel the Archives to stop the closure of the San Francisco facility. This action comes as national Native advocacy organizations have also voiced strong opposition to the planned closures of both the San Francisco and Chicago facilities.

articles.dek: The U.S. Department of Justice has pressed California election officials to prove the citizenship of thousands of voters flagged as potential noncitizens or set aside their ballots ahead of the midterm election.

body: The U.S. Department of Justice has intensified its pressure on California election officials, demanding that thousands of voters identified as potential noncitizens have their citizenship verified or their ballots withheld. Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to state officials, including Secretary of State Shirley Weber and L.A. County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan, requesting a response within 48 hours.

McCotter's letters stated that the Justice Department provided L.A. County with a list of individuals believed to be noncitizens who received mail-in ballots for the Nov. 3 midterm election. Officials were asked to review the list and segregate ballots from individuals whose citizenship cannot be independently confirmed. Voters on the list who had not yet received a ballot should not be sent one until their citizenship is verified, and ballots already returned should not be counted until verification.

California officials criticized the demand, citing concerns about inaccurate federal data that has led to the purging of U.S. citizens from voter rolls in other states. Secretary of State Shirley Weber stated that the Justice Department's actions create chaos and distrust in elections, and that California already has robust laws to ensure only citizens vote. L.A. County officials have not accessed the provided federal data, deeming the thumb drive an insecure medium that conflicts with data privacy protocols.

Election experts have called the demand questionable, particularly given the timing and the history of inaccuracies in similar federal lists. David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, noted that past federal claims about noncitizen voters have been significantly reduced or found to be entirely inaccurate after scrutiny. Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA School of Law, suggested the Justice Department's actions might be legally questionable and could face challenges in court, especially under the National Voter Registration Act's provisions against systematic purges close to an election.

articles.dek: Immigration and Customs Enforcement activities have led to decreased school attendance, halted construction, and instilled fear in agricultural communities across the region.
articles.lead: A reported surge in Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations across California's Central Valley has caused significant disruption, impacting agricultural communities and leading to family separations. The increased enforcement began last week and has sparked confrontations and widespread fear.
articles.takeaway: Immigration and Customs Enforcement activities have led to decreased school attendance, halted construction, and instilled fear in agricultural communities across the region.
body: A reported surge in Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations across California's Central Valley has caused significant disruption, impacting agricultural communities and leading to family separations. The increased enforcement began last week and has sparked confrontations and widespread fear.

In Kerman, the city's mayor confronted ICE agents detaining individuals, stating they were not welcome. The following day, a Fresno resident shot and wounded an ICE agent who was allegedly intoxicated and agitated on the resident's property. Prosecutors have charged the agent with multiple crimes.

Organizers in Madera postponed a cultural festival due to growing fears, and Fresno City Councilmember Miguel Arias reported a substantial drop in school attendance and employee turnout for farm operations, packing sheds, and fields. Construction has also reportedly come to a halt, with very few people visible in the streets.

U.S. Senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, along with U.S. Representative Adam Gray, have written to ICE demanding answers about the purpose, scope, and number of detainees involved in operations in Mendota. Governor Gavin Newsom criticized the increased federal immigration agent presence, calling it a tactic to instill fear and harm communities and the economy.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security stated that ICE enforces the nation's laws and that claims of racial profiling are false, asserting that targets are based on immigration status, not race or ethnicity. However, a review of reported arrests found individuals with recent arrests and others with no apparent criminal record.

articles.headline: As beloved craft breweries close around the state, beer lovers wonder what’s next
articles.dek: In summary Changing consumer tastes, market saturation and rising costs from tariffs has forced the closure of some of the most beloved craft breweries in California. To the dozen regular customers sipping the final ale…
articles.lead: In summary Changing consumer tastes, market saturation and rising costs from tariffs has forced the closure of some of the most beloved craft breweries in California.
articles.takeaway: In summary Changing consumer tastes, market saturation and rising costs from tariffs has forced the closure of some of the most beloved craft breweries in California.
body: In summary Changing consumer tastes, market saturation and rising costs from tariffs has forced the closure of some of the most beloved craft breweries in California.

To the dozen regular customers sipping the final ales and lagers at Prohibition Brewing Company in Vista on a recent Friday night, it not only marks the end of an era, but also raises questions about the future of craft beer.

“There’s a sense of loss. It’s like when ‘Cheers’ closed in the last episode,” said Vista resident Greg Johnson, in a nod to the 1980s sitcom about a neighborhood bar, “where everybody knows your name.” Prohibition will shut its doors this month after the last kegs are drained, making it one of several high-profile brewery closures in San Diego, a region that pioneered the craft brew industry.

Japanese beer-maker Sapporo is selling Stone Brewing, which it acquired in 2022. To the dismay of North County beer lovers, it’s closing the brand’s flagship site in Escondido, Stone Brewing World Bistro & Gardens, with its sprawling complex of terraces and gardens.
“That place was so unique,” one Stone fan wrote on Facebook. “A place to take out of town guests. A place of Escondido pride.” “We are devastated by losing this part of our community,” another wrote.

In August, the 19-year-old Mission Brewing in East Village shuttered its tasting room at the historic, brick Wonder Bread building near Petco Park. At the end of last year Ballast Point Brewing closed its 600-seat bar and restaurant in San Diego’s Miramar district.

articles.headline: Newsom Considers Commuting California's Death Row Sentences
articles.dek: Governor Gavin Newsom is reportedly weighing the commutation of death sentences for 563 inmates, a move that could align California with other states and nations that have abolished capital punishment.
articles.lead: Governor Gavin Newsom has acknowledged considering the commutation of death sentences for the 563 inmates currently on California's death row. This potential action would commute their sentences to life without parole.
articles.takeaway: Governor Gavin Newsom is reportedly weighing the commutation of death sentences for 563 inmates, a move that could align California with other states and nations that have abolished capital punishment.
body: Governor Gavin Newsom has acknowledged considering the commutation of death sentences for the 563 inmates currently on California's death row. This potential action would commute their sentences to life without parole.

Newsom has previously expressed opposition to the death penalty in principle, citing concerns about its flawed implementation and racial bias. He has also dismantled San Quentin's execution chamber, making executions impossible in the state.

While political advisors have reportedly cautioned Newsom against such a move due to potential political repercussions, he has also spoken with prominent death penalty lawyer Bryan Stevenson about the matter. Stevenson has highlighted the U.S.'s position among a small group of countries that retain capital punishment.

Several other states and governors have abolished the death penalty or implemented moratoriums. President Biden also commuted federal death sentences in 2024. Some district attorneys, like Santa Clara County's Jeff Rosen, are also working to withdraw death sentences from cases in their jurisdictions.

Supporters of commutation argue that it would demonstrate a commitment to conscience over political expediency and offer an alternative to a narrative that glorifies violence and death. They believe such a decision could serve as a rejection of a growing cynicism about leadership and a move towards a more just and dignified approach to justice.

attribution.originalTitle: Chabria: The U.S is in the death business. Newsom can change that, and win votes

Bass, seeking a second term, characterized Raman as unprepared to lead, citing a perceived inconsistency in her positions and a struggle to collaborate.
articles.takeaway: Incumbent Mayor Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman traded sharp criticisms on policing, crisis response, and city management in their last televised debate before the Nov.
body: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman engaged in a heated exchange during their final televised debate, focusing on public safety, the city's response to recent fires, and the leadership of the Los Angeles Police Department. Bass, seeking a second term, characterized Raman as unprepared to lead, citing a perceived inconsistency in her positions and a struggle to collaborate.

Raman, in turn, criticized Bass's handling of major incidents, including the Palisades fire and the Boyle Heights warehouse blaze, suggesting the mayor was absent during critical moments. She also raised concerns about a "crisis of trust" at City Hall, arguing that the city cannot afford further mismanagement.

A significant portion of the debate centered on Police Chief Jim McDonnell, who was appointed in 2024. While Raman had previously voted to confirm McDonnell, she now called for his replacement, citing concerns about the LAPD's actions during federal ICE operations and the impact on immigrant communities. Bass countered that removing the chief before the 2028 Olympics would destabilize the police department.

The candidates also debated the effectiveness of Bass's "Inside Safe" program for the homeless, with Raman questioning its accountability and cost-effectiveness. Bass defended the program, noting a decrease in unsheltered homelessness during her term and pointing out that Raman, as head of the housing committee, had approved expenditures for the program.

Bass also addressed a recent controversy involving an Instagram video where Raman's remarks about McDonnell were perceived as inflammatory. Raman stated the video was a mis-edited distortion of her message and was quickly removed.

articles.headline: California Proposition 2 Aims to Bolster Rainy Day Fund
articles.dek: A bipartisan proposal seeks to double the state's budget reserves to mitigate the impact of economic downturns and reduce the need for program cuts.
articles.lead: State leaders from both Democratic and Republican parties have found common ground on a measure designed to stabilize California's budget. Proposition 2, as it is being called, aims to increase the state's savings for economic downturns.
articles.takeaway: A bipartisan proposal seeks to double the state's budget reserves to mitigate the impact of economic downturns and reduce the need for program cuts.
body: State leaders from both Democratic and Republican parties have found common ground on a measure designed to stabilize California's budget. Proposition 2, as it is being called, aims to increase the state's savings for economic downturns.

California's economy is known for its size and dynamism, but also for its volatility, ranking fifth nationally in revenue fluctuations. Despite this, the state's budget reserves are relatively small, ranking 29th in the nation. This imbalance often leads to significant cuts in essential services like healthcare, higher education, public safety, and social safety nets during economic challenges.

Proposition 2 proposes to double the size of the state's rainy day fund. This measure would require California to save more during periods of strong revenue growth, thereby creating a larger cushion to absorb the impact of future economic downturns without necessitating immediate, painful budget reductions.

The initiative builds upon a framework approved by voters in 2014 and incorporates lessons learned from over a decade of experience with the existing reserve fund. The proposal was developed with input from budget experts, including the Legislative Analyst's Office, the Department of Finance, independent fiscal analysts, and business leaders.

Supporters argue that a larger rainy day fund will enhance California's fiscal credibility, enabling it to weather economic storms more effectively, borrow at lower rates, and provide greater confidence to families and businesses that the state can maintain its commitments during challenging economic times.

attribution.originalTitle: One area Democrats, GOP agree: California needs a larger rainy day fund

faqs.question: What is the main goal of Proposition 2?
faqs.answer: Proposition 2 aims to double the size of California's rainy day fund to better manage budget volatility and avoid deep cuts to state programs during economic downturns.

faqs.answer: The proposal was developed by budget experts, including the Legislative Analyst's Office, the Department of Finance, independent fiscal experts, and business leaders, with bipartisan support from state leaders.

body: Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman, a candidate for mayor, has frequently shifted her stances on significant policy issues. Since 2021, Raman voted more than 60 times against measures to ban homeless encampments in public areas. However, after announcing her mayoral bid, she stated that as mayor, she would not oppose council efforts to create new no-camping zones.

During her 2020 City Council campaign, Raman advocated for defunding the police. Two years later, she voted for a nearly 3% increase in the Los Angeles Police Department's budget, allocating an additional $82 million. More recently, she voted against Mayor Karen Bass's request to add 170 police officers, citing budget concerns. Weeks after launching her mayoral campaign, Raman declared that city leaders must maintain the LAPD's size.

Raman also initially supported Measure ULA, a tax on real estate sales above $5.4 million, downplaying concerns about its impact on apartment construction. She later reversed her position, stating the tax has negatively affected apartment construction and requires an overhaul, arguing that a policy worsening a housing shortage cannot address a housing crisis.

Her campaign team defends these shifts, attributing them to new information, changed circumstances, or a re-evaluation of issues. Opponents, including Mayor Bass, have criticized Raman's changing positions, with some colleagues questioning her core principles. Raman has stated that her thinking evolves based on new facts and that she takes responsibility for mistakes.

Raman's evolving positions extend to her endorsement of Mayor Bass for a second term, which she later rescinded when she entered the mayoral race herself. She explained her initial endorsement as a strategy to secure resources for her district. Critics have characterized these shifts as opportunistic, while supporters view her willingness to re-examine positions as a strength.

body: This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here. See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred In rural Modoc County, in California’s remote northeast corner, Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton donned a beige cowboy hat and climbed atop a horse.

Riding through a grassy field, with his dress shoes in the stirrups, Hilton lamented to a camera that California was “completely being ruined by killjoy bureaucrats” who put too many rules on fun stuff like beach fire pits and bars that stay open extra late.

In coastal San Luis Obispo County, Hilton boarded a bright yellow dune buggy at the Oceano Dunes State Vehicular Recreation Area and called the California Coastal Commission “idiots” for trying to end off-road beach driving.
And in the Central Valley, he waved the ceremonial green flag at a stock car race at the Madera Speedway, where he was named grand marshal of the annual Harvest Classic.

(The designation caused a minor uproar, prompting the operator of the racetrack to make a fake online concession menu that offered a hot dog and soda for $6 for Republicans and $17.50 for Democrats.) If it seems like Hilton — the British immigrant and former Fox News talk show host — is just about everywhere, taking just about every media interview that comes his way, well, that’s the point, he says.

He has logged thousands of miles on the proverbial campaign trail, visiting all 58 counties in his quest to lead the nation’s most populous state, where no Republican has been elected to statewide office in 20 years.
